# Preface {.unnumbered}

A student came to me some years ago with a hard disk of RNA-seq data and a deadline.
She had been taught molecular biology thoroughly and had generated the samples
herself. What she had not been taught was what to do with sixty gigabytes of
compressed text. She had spent a fortnight trying to open a FASTQ file in a
spreadsheet.

That gap — between producing biological data and being able to do anything with it —
is the reason this book exists. It is a gap that has widened every year since
high-throughput sequencing became routine. Sequencing a bacterial genome is now a
service you can buy; interpreting it is not. The limiting reagent in a great deal of
modern biology is no longer the experiment but the analysis.

The usual remedies have not worked well. Bioinformatics is often taught either as
computer science with biological examples, which loses the biologists, or as a tour
of web tools, which produces users who can click through an interface but cannot
tell when its output is wrong. Neither approach produces someone who can take an
unfamiliar dataset and make defensible sense of it.

This book takes a third approach, which is simply to do the work. Every concept is
introduced because it is needed for a decision in an actual analysis. Every method
is demonstrated on real data that comes with the book. Every piece of output you see
was generated by the code printed above it, on the data described beside it. When a
tool cannot be run inside the book, the command is shown as it was actually run, and
its real output is quoted.

## What this book assumes {.unnumbered}

It assumes you have seen the central dogma before and can be reminded rather than
taught. It assumes no programming experience whatsoever. It assumes you have a
computer with a terminal and the patience to type into it.

It does not assume you are a computer scientist, and it does not try to make you
one. There is no complexity analysis here, and the algorithms are derived only to
the depth that changes how you use them. There is, however, a sustained insistence
on one point that is genuinely computational: that an analysis you cannot repeat is
not a result. Scripts, environments, version control and recorded provenance appear
from Chapter 1 and never go away.

## What this book is not {.unnumbered}

It is not a reference manual. Tools change; the documentation for any one of them
will be more current than this book by the time you read it. What is durable is the
reasoning — why you align before you count, why a p-value from a genome-wide test
needs correcting, why an annotation inherited from a homologue is a hypothesis.
That reasoning is what I have tried to write down.

Nor is it a clinical text. Chapter 13 covers variant interpretation and
pharmacogenomics because they are now part of the field, but patient-facing
decisions belong to accredited laboratories and qualified clinicians, and the
chapter says so.

## A note on where this was written {.unnumbered}

Much of my own work has been done in settings where compute is shared, bandwidth is
intermittent and software licences are out of reach. That shapes the book. Every
tool used here is free and open source. Every dataset is small enough to download
over a poor connection. Nothing requires a cluster, though Chapter 5 explains how to
use one when you have access. Genomics will only be as global as its methods are
accessible, and I have tried to write accordingly.

## Acknowledgement of the reader {.unnumbered}

Bioinformatics rewards stubbornness more than talent. The first time an aligner
fails with an error you have never seen, it will be tempting to conclude that you
are not the sort of person who does this. You will be wrong. Everyone who works in
this field spends a substantial fraction of their time confused, and the difference
between those who continue and those who do not is mostly a willingness to read the
error message carefully and try again.

*Umar Ahmad*
*Bauchi, Nigeria*
